title: Char Array vs Char Pointer
concept: A modifiable chalkboard (array) vs an immutable stone tablet (pointer)

steps.title: Including stdio.h header
steps.explanation:
This header is needed to use `printf`.

This lesson covers the difference in mutability between `char arrays` and `char pointers`.

steps.title: Starting main function
steps.explanation:
The main frame is created.

We will compare how the same string representation differs in storage location and mutability.

steps.title: Method 1: Char array declaration (modifiable)
steps.explanation:
`char arr[] = "Hello";` copies the string into the array.

Array elements can be modified just like regular memory.

steps.title: Modifying array contents
steps.explanation:
Changing an element with `arr[0] = ...` actually modifies the string content.

This is because arrays are writable storage.

steps.title: Printing the modified array
steps.explanation: The modified array string is printed, confirming the change took effect.

steps.title: Method 2: Char pointer declaration (read-only)
steps.explanation:
`char *ptr = "World";` points to a string literal's address.

Literals reside in read-only memory and cannot be modified.

steps.title: Printing the pointer's string
steps.explanation: Read-only strings can still be printed normally.

steps.title: What if you try to modify it? (Crash!)
steps.explanation:
Attempting to write to a string literal can cause a runtime error.

Pointer strings should always be treated as read-only.

steps.title: Program termination
steps.explanation:
The program ends with `return 0;`.

Summary: Array strings are modifiable; literal pointer strings are not.

quiz.question: If you need to modify a string's contents, how should you declare it?
quiz.explanation:
Declaring with brackets (`[]`) creates a modifiable copy on the stack (or data segment).
Pointing to a string constant with (`*`) means you cannot modify it.

misconceptions.wrong: char *s = "A"; is stored on the heap
misconceptions.correct: It is stored in the code (text) segment, not the heap.
misconceptions.why:
Unless you use `malloc`, it is not on the heap.
It is a constant stored alongside the program code.

keyTakeaway: Need to modify? Use `[]` (array). Read-only? Use `*` (pointer). Know the difference.
